speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister in connection with two articles in the current issue of the Financial Post. Is it correct, as reported in these articles, that the Prime Minister recently sent a letter of protest or objection to the President of the United States against the give-away program of the surplus agricultural products of the United States? If so, when was that letter of protest sent? Has the President replied to it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I saw the two items in the Financial Post to which the hon. gentleman has referred and I was very much surprised to see them. I do not think I should either confirm or deny that there have been any such letters. There are occasions when it is necessary for those who have responsibility to have confidential conferences, and this method of publishing certain statements and then getting a confirmation or denial would make the system of confidential interviews or confidential correspondence lose practically its whole value. If there is a statement that there has been confidential correspondence and that it is not to be disclosed, there are people who are so suspicious as to think there must be something to hide in that kind of correspondence. I think it is highly desirable that those who are in responsible positions can have these confidential communications without there being this publicity that is not helpful to the ultimate results that are sought to be achieved.
I am sorry that I feel I should not comply with the hon. gentleman's request to either confirm or deny what is in this report. I have had confidential communications, either orally or in writing, on many occasions concerning many different subjects with the President of the United States. There is nothing that should be hidden in those confidential exchanges, but they were directed to achieving results which would be more difficult to achieve if there could not be these
frank, confidential exchanges of views. I am quite sure if I attempted to publicize things that both the President and I consider as confidential it would destroy the basis upon which we have been having these confidential exchanges.

Mr. Speaker, this goes further than that. On January 24, 1957, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when asked whether there had been any protest, used these words which appear at the bottom of page 589 of Hansard for that date:
We do not file our protests in writing; we file them through the committee.
The question as to whether or not there was a protest made to the President of the United States is one in respect of which this house has the right to information. This is not a personal conversation, this is a protest on behalf of the people of Canada, if indeed such a protest was made; and for the Prime Minister to take the stand that when it is convenient not to give information to parliament the method of going about it is simply to make a protest-
Order.

*-in a whisper is not in keeping with the rights of parliament. I ask the Prime Minister once more for this information, because too often throughout this session the house has been denied information to which it is entitled.
Rubbish.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made no official protest as Prime Minister of Canada to the President of the United States.

speechtext:
know it is common in Canada to assume that if certain taxes were reduced the cost of production would decline and there would therefore perhaps be greater employment. It is easy to suggest that excise taxes are the cause of unemployment. I would not want to say that was or was not the fact in the motor car industry, but if there are any effects of the fiscal policy being felt by the motor car industry in particular it should be borne in mind that taxation is very widespread in Canada, and in so far as it is possible to do so it is the desire of the government that taxation should be borne by the taxpayers in as proper a manner as can be devised.
With particular reference to the motor car industry I have already indicated, and the house on numerous occasions has discussed the question, what affects the sale of motor cars, or at any rate the delivery of motor cars, at this time from the manufacturer to the motor car dealer. I do have an announcement to make in that regard.
Automobile dealers are reluctant in this period before the budget to accept deliveries of cars from the manufacturers. At times when the tax on automobiles is reduced, dealers may have inventory on hand on which tax has been paid, and in order to avoid loss they naturally try to arrange to have on hand as few cars as possible.
To avoid or minimize disruption in the marketing processes in the industry I have decided to announce now my intention to recommend to the house later in the session a minor technical amendment to the Excise Tax Act which I think will solve the problem of the slow-down of car deliveries.
At present excise tax on an automobile is payable by the manufacturer when it is delivered to the dealer or, if imported, when the customs entry is passed. It is proposed to amend the law so that excise tax will not be payable until ownership of the car passes to the dealer. This change, which will be effective as from February 1, will enable the dealer to accept delivery of a car still owned by the manufacturer, but it will not be a tax-paid car until after title to the property has passed to the dealer. This seems to be a sensible arrangement in the case of large items such as automobiles, where the storage problem can be difficult. The ordinary rule calling for payment of tax on physical delivery will continue to apply to other items subject to excise tax.
I need scarcely add that this announcement of a proposal for a minor technical change in the law relating to the time of payment of tax can in no sense be regarded as

any indication of whether, in the forthcoming budget, there will be any change in the rate of tax on automobiles either up or down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
May I suggest to hon. members, for the good of all of us and I suppose for the good of parliament, that we should refrain at question time from engaging in debate. I have on previous occasions outlined the rules with respect to the asking of questions, and also with respect to the answering of questions. The minute we go beyond the reasonable limits of those rules and engage in debating certain questions and answers, well, what happens is that the atmosphere gets heated up and we have all kinds of interjections going across the floor of the house, because at this moment members are not entitled to make lengthy speeches to express themselves. They try to concentrate in a few sentences what they would like to say perhaps in 40 minutes. Therefore you have these capsule, concentrated expressions which really do not add any advantage to the house or to the members who express them.
I would ask hon. members within reasonable limits to keep within the rules. They know what they are; I am sure they do. Whether they want to follow them as they are is a different proposition. As far as I am concerned, once the question is put- first I have to listen to it-I look to the person to whom the question is addressed and in 99 per cent of the cases he is on his feet to reply.

Inquiries of the Ministry
My position with respect to question time is this. As long as it is the wish of many hon. members in the house to ask questions in which they include a great deal of debatable material and if it is the wish of those who reply, probably because of the type of question they get, to include in their answers a lot of debatable material, it is not to be expected that the person who put the question originally is not going to ask a supplementary question to get back precisely at the type of debatable material which was in the answer. Therefore it is a vicious circle, and it is enough to make anyone dizzy, especially the Speaker.

I would like to say, first of all, that we of the C.C.F. party have endorsed this method of orderly marketing Canadian wheat over the years, and we support the proposed extension of this act for another five years. We do feel, however, that it would add to the significance of the government's support of this method of operating, and of selling Canadian wheat, if the minister could see fit to bring in a bill which would make the act permanent. We feel that the support of the western farmers and farm organizations is such that they are now completely sold on this method of marketing through the Canadian wheat board, and would support any action taken to make this legislation permanent.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, there is misapprehension with regard to this method of marketing wheat, and with regard to the fact that all the operations of the Canadian wheat board are paid for by the farmers themselves. The farmer pays the marketing charges; he pays for country storage and terminal storage; he pays the cost of the wheat board's operations and also the interest charged by the banks for the money used. In addition the farmers pay, out of the proceeds of their sales, for the grading of that wheat, for drying charges, and for all administrative costs. Thus, Mr. Speaker, I wanted it clearly understood at the outset by all hon. members who do not understand the operations of the board that the farmer pays for the Canadian wheat board; he pays the cost of this method of selling his wheat.
I think, sir, it would be well if I were to make a brief review of the history of the Canadian wheat board, because some hon. members may have the impression-and sometimes the impression has been created in the country-that the mint has been used excessively to subsidize Canadian wheat producers. That is completely erroneous. In 1935, when the Canadian wheat board was set up, a farmer had the choice of selling his wheat through the wheat board or on the open market. Ever since the early years when the Winnipeg grain exchange gambled

on the wheat crop, the farmers and their organizations had been trying to encourage the government to institute another form of marketing. The consequences of the old method of operation were that the western farmer often got a low price for his product. So from 1935 onward the farmers generally supported the Canadian wheat board and operated through that agency.
It was not until September of 1943, Mr. Speaker, that the wheat board became the sole marketing agency for western wheat, and it is somewhat significant to note that the price of wheat went up on the date the federal Liberal government decided, not by legislation but by order in council, to put all Canadian wheat marketing under the sole agency of the Canadian wheat board. As of that date wheat on the grain exchange had jumped the maximum of 14 cents, and they stepped in by order in council and put all Canadian wheat under the control of the wheat board.
That was the situation until 1948 when, of course, oats and barley were also brought within the sphere of the board's operations. We in this group support the organization and, as I have indicated, farmers throughout the country support the work the Canadian wheat board is doing. We have never at any time tried to indicate or promote measures which might in any way jeopardize this method of marketing. However, we do feel that the western farmer is caught in a cost-price squeeze.
Some days ago the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre tried to indicate that we in this group had been misrepresenting the situation of the western farmer. I do not think, myself, that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is in his seat at the present time, comes into this house and makes a statement about being out in Saskatchewan and driving with a farmer who owns a Cadillac, this should be taken as an indication that all western farmers are driving Cadillacs. Nor when we find the Minister of Agriculture saying that the only farmer in western Canada whom he found to be hard up was one who had to sell his airplane, should we take such stories too seriously. These are gross exaggerations of the present position of the western farmers and I daresay there are few if any farmers in western Canada such as those two gentlemen alluded to.
I think, Mr. Speaker, it would be more appropriate if instead of listening to such statements we were to listen to statements made by people who have the interests of the farmers at heart, and which perhaps deal with the situation of the western farmer more fairly.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
I should like to refer to certain statements of Mr. Wesson, head of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. In the Western Producer of January 17 there is the following:
In point of fact the squeeze is becoming daily more pronounced as the differential between what the farmer sells and the goods he has to buy continues with every passing month to widen. Mr. Wesson, who is not noted for exaggerated or irresponsible statements in such matters, says flatly: "The continued high cost of things needed to operate a farm and to maintain the farm family is putting the farmer in an impossible position."
In my opinion this is conclusive evidence that the very reputable head of the Saskatchewan wheat pool has put forward the situation facing the western farmer concisely and definitely. I should also like to say that those of us in this group have tried to indicate that the prices of wheat and the other things the farmer has to sell have been going down generally since the war years and the cost of the things he has to buy has been going up, placing him in a cost-price squeeze.
In that regard it is interesting to note that during the period from 1930 to 1939 the farmers received 6.1 per cent of the national income. During the period from 1946 to 1954 inclusive the farmers' share of the national income dropped until they were only getting 5.6 per cent, even less than the average in the depression years of the thirties. Therefore it is obvious that today the western Canada farmer is in a cost-price squeeze.
I believe that the government has used the Canadian wheat board as a means to stabilize price levels in Canada and perhaps in some measure to stop inflation. I do not mean to say that the western farmer does not agree with this method of marketing but I should like to point out that the farmer took a lower price for his wheat during the war years and also during the four year period of the British wheat agreement under which Canada sold to Britain in the first two years 160 million bushels of wheat and 140 million bushels in the second two years at a price of $1.55 a bushel when on the world market the farmer could have got a much higher price.
In other words, during the war years and since the farmers have held the price line against inflation. It is also true that in the war years the farmer not only subsidized Canadian consumers by taking $1.25 a bushel for the 60 million to 70 million bushels of wheat consumed in Canada in the form of bread and flour but also as a taxpayer paid his share of the subsidy of 78 cents a bushel paid to millers during that period. Rather than the farmer crying for hand-outs, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) said on Friday last, rather than it being a case of those of us in this group

Canadian Wheat Board Act crying for hand-outs on behalf of the farmer, all that the farmer wants is economic justice.
It seems to me that something can be done about this problem. We have suggested that farmers should have parity prices. It seems ridiculous to me that consumers should have to take a trimming in buying a loaf of bread having in mind the price that the farmer is getting for his wheat. I noticed the other day that bread went up another cent a loaf in the city of Ottawa but the farmer is getting the same price for his wheat as he got ten years ago. As a matter of fact, there is only 3 cents' worth of bread flour in a 20 ounce loaf of bread for which the consumer today has to pay over 20 cents a loaf.
The farmer has not been getting a fair or equitable deal with respect to the prices of his wheat and the other commodities he sells. The Canadian wheat board is a good idea but that is no reason why we cannot make it a better organization. That is no reason why the government cannot undertake policies such as we have advocated which will receive the full support of the western farmer. I say that if the government refuses to do so and tries to fetter the Canadian wheat board so that it will not be a satisfactory marketing agency for western wheat there is no single thing which will do more to lessen the support of the western farmer for the wheat board.
We in this group have made certain recommendations and I will deal with them in a minute. First, I want to refer to exports of Canadian wheat. I think this is a serious matter. We have the finest wheat in the world but our sales have deteriorated and we have not got our share of the world market. In my opinion that is a serious matter for everybody in Canada, including consumers. Last evening the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) endeavoured to deal with Canada's percentage of wheat sales. As found at page 1037 of Hansard, he said:
Actually we are in no worse position today than we were in the years since the end of the war.
That is not a very satisfactory thing to have to say in the house. I think we should be trying to undertake policies which would result in our being in a more favourable position. Taking the figures found in the report of the Canadian wheat board for the crop year 1955-56, I find that in the 1945-46 crop year Canada exported 373 million bushels of wheat, or 43 per cent of the world export trade. In 1953-54 we exported only 278 million bushels or only 32 per cent of the world export trade. Still dealing with those two years I find that in 1945-46 total world exports amounted to 868 million bushels whereas in 1953-54 they amounted to 
869 million bushels, a variation of only one million in world exports of wheat. Yet our export trade has dropped from 43 per cent to 32 per cent. Surely that is something that should concern the government when, as I say, we have the finest wheat in the world to sell.
With a group of members of the house I went to Washington two years ago and found that the greatest part of the large stocks of wheat in store under the commodity credit corporation in that country consisted of inferior, low grade wheat. We were told that much of the wheat was not fit for milling and would only be milled if there was a real scarcity of better milling wheat.
Many people have talked loosely about the method of disposal of the United States wheat crop. I recall seeing a news report last winter when the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) was in the constituency of Assiniboia. He was reported as having said that our suggestion that we should enter into the same kind of deals and contracts as the United States government was silly. I think the capitalist government of the United States is a pretty hard-headed type of capitalist government and I do not think they are following any methods in the disposal of their wheat which are not in the interests of the farmer and in the interests of the United States. Their policy for the disposal of wheat is not simply a give-away program. I should like to refer to public law 480 of the United States and, incidentally, there are three different methods for the disposal of wheat under that law.
For example, under Title I of Public Law 480, as recorded here in the Canadian wheat board report we find the following:
. . . surplus agricultural commodities may be sold for the currency of the importing country and the funds so acquired are utilized for market development, purchase of strategic materials, military procurement, purchase of goods for other countries, grants for multilateral trade and economic development, loans for economic development within the recipient country and international educational exchange.
It seems to me that in that type of deal there is much merit. Then, of course, under the disposal plan, Title II, we find the following:
Under this law surplus agricultural commodities may be donated to relieve famine and disaster to any nation friendly to the United States, or to friendly, needy populations without regard to the friendliness of their government.
Again it seems that these are worthy types of deals to enter into when any country has a surplus rather than have them spoil as they did in the thirties and I think they should receive the support of those who have the needs and the welfare of people at heart.
We are not letting the surpluses spoil. We are selling for cash.

During the crop year 1955-56 barter programs played an important part in United States grain exports.
When hon. members try to mislead the public by saying that the United States wheat disposal programs are all give-away programs, I think that such a statement cannot be substantiated.
They are heavily subsidized.

Those of us in this group have advocated certain things which should be undertaken by this federal government. I am going to say this. I do not feel that it is fair for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to hide behind the skirts of the Canadian wheat board. During the course of this session we were told that the government has not seen fit to appoint a transport controller because of the actions of some naughty boys on this side of the house. I submit that this is a very weak excuse. The wheat board is being blamed unjustly simply because the government has not seen fit to appoint a transport controller who would bring orderly marketing in the west. I feel that the government has not acted in this regard because it realizes it is powerless to assist the wheat board in securing orderly marketing in the west as long as it continues to follow its present marketing policies.
I now wish to spend a few moments dealing with marketing and our markets. Last evening I listened to a speech by a member on the other side who assured us that we would continue to have our markets, but I am of the opinion we are losing our markets and will continue to lose them until our policies are changed. We often hear the grain marketing policies of the United States criticized in this house. Whether we like it or not we must admit we are losing our markets to the United States. Our government has refused to accept the currencies of other countries and has refused to enter into barter deals. We are told by leading government officials that huge reserves of grain in Canada are a good thing, but who pays for those huge reserves, who pays to keep them? Is it the people of Canada as a whole? No, the brunt of the burden is borne by the farmers themselves.
In recent years we have developed a large export market for grain with Japan and in this connection I should like to quote from the Wheat Pool Budget of November 16. The title of the article is "Who Cares about Grain Markets?" and it reads:
Trade Minister Howe recently predicted that Japan will probably become our best customer.

Canadian Wheat Board Act Beyond question this market is only being held and developed because of our growing imports from Japan.
To the Canadian farmer and many others this increased trade and better market for wheat is sound business. To the Financial Times and the Canadian manufacturers, however, it is a different story. On November 2 the Times decried the trend toward a balanced trade with Japan and bewailed the harsh effects on Canadian manufacturers. It revived the old cry that they were not receiving sufficient protection against the products of low priced labour.
It is evident that interests in Canada are quite prepared to sacrifice agriculture in order to maintain their rigidly protected special preserve in the home market where they can make big profits. Canadian exporters, particularly the farmers, must buy the goods they require from protected Canadian manufacturers at much higher prices than are charged elsewhere. At the same time they are penalized in the marketing of their own goods abroad, not only by foreign tariffs, but also by the resistance of the Canadian manufacturer to a balanced trade. In short, some section of the Canadian people must pay a special levy to another, but themselves are not to be permitted to make a living. The Financial Times may be the mouthpiece for high finance but it has a very distorted idea of sound economy.
Unless we start buying from countries to which we sell our agricultural products we cannot hope to maintain our export sales to them. The farmers are forced to place their grain through the wheat board upon a highly competitive market. Early this year it was announced that the United States had agreed to make foreign aid available to Poland and she will likely give the same privilege to other satellite countries. Last year Canada sold Poland 14 million bushels of wheat. We are likely to lose this market if we maintain our orthodox system of marketing. Last year we sold wheat to Russia and satellite countries, much of which was financed on short-term loans. So far this year we have heard of no sales of grain to communist countries. What is happening to our markets there? What is happening to our markets in India and Pakistan? New markets must be found and established markets must be held if we are to get rid of our surplus.
Cash advances on farm-stored grain have been urged from time to time in this house, Last year the $1,500 bank loan bill was passed but it proved to be of little or no help to the farmer. Some way must soon be found either to permit farmers to market their grain, or if we wish to continue our level of production there must be a system of cash advances handled through some government agency other than the wheat board.
Speaking in this debate last Friday the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) discussed the two-price system for agricultural products. He pointed out that most agricultural organizations were requesting such a system. In its brief presented to the federal-provincial agricultural conference

held in Ottawa December 3 to December 6, 1956, the interprovincial farm union council had this to say:
We believe that immediate consideration should be given to a program of parity prices on the domestic market and adequate support prices under exports. The Canadian farmer has not participated in Canada's economic boom, but presently finds himself subsidizing the Canadian consumer. If subsidized food is what we want, then the taxpayers of Canada as a whole should bear the cost. Agricultural producers have borne the cost for longer than they can afford.
And further down:
Action must be taken to increase prices to producers. A parity price on the domestic market related to production costs and Canadian living standards, we consider a reasonable request. We recognize that in order for our grain to compete on the export market, it must be sold at competitive prices. Present world market prices do not give the Canadian producer a sufficient return to meet his present costs of operation. Therefore, we recommend that deficiency payments or a support price structure be instituted to cover exports and return to producers their fair share of the national income.
That brief was in support of the plea which the hon. member for Acadia has made over the past several years for the introduction of a two-price system for all agricultural products grown in Canada.
Another matter which has caused great concern among the farmers of Alberta is the special quota of three bushels per seeded acre for barley. This quota was not in operation in our province but it was in effect in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. While we are prepared to admit that the officials of the Canadian wheat board must have sufficient stocks on hand to meet necessary export commitments at all times, we do feel that iri this particular instance the barley producers of Alberta have been discriminated against. It is to be hoped that a demand for barley at the west coast terminals will soon arise so that the Alberta producers will be able to take advantage of this additional special quota.
Last year it was my privilege to attend the farmers union of Alberta convention in Edmonton. Farm problems were discussed at length by the delegates attending that convention and several resolutions with respect to grain policy were passed. The convention asked for such things as the inclusion of the marketing of flax and rye under the Canadian wheat board; it asked for the extension of bilateral agreements; that all grains used on the domestic market be sold at parity prices; that a uniform quota policy be adopted on an annual basis. The convention asked for cash advances and that such advances be the full initial payment. It asked that advances be paid on the basis of one-half of the deliverable grain and that all administration and interest charges be

borne by the government of Canada. It asked that these advances be repayable on the basis of one-half the value of each delivery made by the farmer.
The convention also discussed the setting up of a food bank and also the distribution of box cars, that they be so allocated that farmers may deliver their grain to the elevators of their choice. Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention at this time to spend very long on this question. I have spoken on it before and other members of our party have stated our position most clearly. Therefore, I do not intend to repeat many of the points raised by the members of this group. However, I wish to say at the beginning, so that there will be no misunderstanding the position which we take on this matter, that we intend to support Bill No. 9, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act to extend the operations of the wheat board for another five years. I think the reason for that is evident. The reason most members in this house, and particularly those from western Canada, are in agreement with extending the operations of the wheat board for another five years is that we do not want to go back to the open-market methods of years ago. Those of us from the west can well remember the state of affairs which existed in those times. Nearly all the bills which the farmer had

accumulated came due in the fall immediately after threshing and invariably the price on the open-market system was the lowest for the year. The farmers were compelled to sell their grain at that time to meet their obligations and therefore they took the lowest price possible.
It is true that when you look at the statistics you will see that the average price of grain over the year might have been fairly good, but certainly the cash income that the farmer received was at a very low level. We do not want to see those conditions return.
The wheat board has been in operation now for some 14 years. As far as the western farmers are concerned, it has been proven that they obtained a far better average price during those 14 years than they ever had before the board came into existence. They would not have received that price had the wheat board not been in existence in the last 14 years.
The wheat board-and I agree with this- has had a stabilizing effect on the marketing of wheat. We were glad to see oats and barley included in the operations of the board and we would like the government to go farther and extend the operations of the board to flax and rye. We would also like to see the government take a step to make the wheat board legislation permanent.
On February 1, when the minister spoke about the operations of the wheat board, he went to great lengths to explain that the wheat board had been a success. He pointed out-and I think properly so-that all of the farmers and all of the farm organizations were in support of the continuation of the wheat board. If that is so-and I think it is so -then the government should take immediate steps to put the wheat board under permanent legislation. What is the use of year after year, or every five years at the most, renewing the life of the board or bringing down an amendment to extend the life of the wheat board for a further period of time? If it has been proven that it is a success- and we all agree that it has been-then I think we should put the board under permanent legislation. If that were done it would eliminate most of the criticism that comes from those who support open-market operations in their continuous effort to try to undermine the wheat board and have it done away with so that the old practices may continue to the benefit of the favoured few and to the detriment of agriculture and all those connected with it.

Canadian Wheat Board Act may at times become impatient with us because we repeat our arguments in favour of western agriculture. But this is a serious problem as far as agriculture is concerned. The government did take a step in the right direction not long ago when it agreed to pay the storage charges on all wheat in excess of 178 million bushels. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, when the government took that step it acknowledged to the country, and particularly to the farmers, that the policies which it had been pursuing over the last years have certainly not been justified and the forcing of the farmers to pay the carrying charges on the surplus was something that should not have happened.
After having acknowledged their shortcomings in this respect by agreeing to pay storage on all wheat in excess of 178 million bushels, it does seem to me that the government has a responsibility to compensate the farmers of this country for the losses which they have incurred because of the government's failure to recognize the problem and make amends in that respect. I am not arguing about who should do it- that is the government's responsibility. But certainly it should be done. It is common knowledge in this house, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of western Canada are finding very great difficulty in getting the cash that is necessary for them to finance their farm operations. In fact, almost everyone has had to go into debt in order to get money to carry them over, and last fall, when these debts became due, people still had no money -in fact, in a great many cases, they had not paid the farm loans which they had received the year before. And how can you expect them to pay when they cannot sell their grain? It seems to be putting a farmer into an impossible position when he must of necessity accumulate debts in order to carry on his farming operations. Then fall comes; the farmer threshes his grain-and has no place to sell it. And still we need the surpluses, at a time when people all over the world are starving. Surely, this is not a time to consider reducing these surpluses. However, the government thinks nothing should be done in this respect.
Another unfair condition which existed last fall was that farmers were not able to sell very much wheat. This matter came up before the agriculture committee, and Mr. Milner, who was transport controller at that time, pointed out to us that he had had difficulty, particularly with the C.P.R., in getting cars allocated to points where he thought they should have been sent.

I had some of these points in my constituency, and last year they had only delivered up to about a five-bushel quota, and some not even that. When I wrote to Mr. Milner about it-I was referring at that time particularly to the Standard area in my riding -he said action would be taken, and I must give him credit for sending some box cars in there immediately. That brought the quota up in some points to five bushels. But he did say, too, that he would see that this particular area would have continued special attention. Of course, nothing further was done.
The problem that these people face is that they did not sell more than five bushels last year. Now they start again this year under a handicap. Sure, they had a 300-bushel initial delivery. Then the quota started, and some of them to this day have only got two and three-bushel quotas.
How is it possible for agriculture to carry on under these conditions? I think we have reached a point, Mr. Speaker, where the government should recognize the importance of making some provision for giving cash advances on farm-stored grain in order that our farmers may get some cash with which to carry on.
I shall not continue further, Mr. Speaker, because I am sure you would not allow me to do so, anyway-I see my time is nearly expired-and it is not my intention to prolong the proceedings on this occasion. It is certainly not my intention to hold up the present passage of this bill, because we want to see it go through. I hope, however, that the government will take into consideration some of the serious problems I have brought to their attention, because agriculture needs some assistance. Farmers are not asking for charity by any means; they are only asking that this government should take some action that would give them a cash return so that they can pay the many obligations that they are required to meet.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to extend the term of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, giving it an additional life of five years. As one who represents a grain-producing community I would like to say a word or two in connection with it.
Many speakers have risen and suggested that this should remain as permanent legislation. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that as long as the farmers in western Canada want the wheat board system of marketing, this act, when it comes up again in another five years for consideration, will be further renewed. This government has embarked on this policy of the wheat board system of
Canadian Wheat Board Act marketing and I do not think there is any danger whatsoever that this act would not be extended.
Furthermore, the present procedure gives an opportunity to review and discuss the operations of this board, and to make suggestions, as we have been doing. As I say, I have no fears that the wheat board method of marketing will not be continued in the future-provided it has not been scuttled in the meantime through the adoption of certain suggestions whereby an extra load will be put on the shoulders of the board in addition to the heavy load which it is already carrying. I propose to say something about that shortly.
Another point which has been raised is the question of the inequality of delivery opportunities, and this is, of course, a very difficult problem. In dealing with it I can probably do no better than to pass on the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he spoke at the Saskatchewan wheat pool convention held at Regina on the 9th November last. This is what he had to say in connection with it:
I know that you are concerned about what might be termed the inequalities of delivery opportunities. This is an extremely difficult problem and the wheat board is doing its best to cope with it. But it cannot perform miracles and it cannot afford to put equality of delivery opportunities ahead of selling wheat. The wheat board had to take advantage of every demand which came along. This demand, in many cases, was for specific kinds of grain and grades of grain, and not all delivery points in the west could supply these requirements in equal volume. Therefore, the wheat board had to be selective in its shipping policy in order to move to terminals the grades of grain required to meet demand. This caused some inequalities in delivery quotas, but I thought the wheat board was wise in shipping the grains and grades which could be moved promptly into the domestic or export market. Only by taking this action did we reach the volume of exports and the volume of sales which were attained in the past crop year.
Then the minister goes on to say:
Let me give you one example. When the crop year 1955-56 began, the board had very substantial holdings of low grade wheat-No. 5, No. 6 and feed wheat-amounting to well over 100 million bushels. By the end of the crop year the board had sold all these stocks and had to look to the 1956 crop for additional supplies of these grades. The selling of this volume of low-grade wheat could not have been accomplished except by taking every step possible to move these particular grades into selling positions.
As I say, there are inequalities of delivery opportunities. It is a serious problem at certain points in western Canada but I think the complete answer is given in the statement made by the minister. I think history will record that during these trying years the wheat board had to stand the acid test with respect to its performance in the face of great obstacles. It faces great difficulties

Canadian Wheat Board Act in the marketing of our grain, greater particularly in the last two years than at any time since the end of the last war.
What have been some of the problems that have confronted the wheat board? Briefly they have been these. First of all, we have had superabundant crops. During the last six years we have had five of the largest crops in the history of this country and the world was simply not in a position to absorb the record crop production in Canada with the result that some had to be carried over on farms and in elevators. That was one problem over which the government and the wheat board had no control.
The second problem was the heavy subsidization of wheat importing countries throughout the world. Some of these importing countries encouraged production at home by means of high internal prices. Again that is something over which the government and the wheat board had no control.
The third problem, and a very serious one, is the surplus disposal methods followed by the United States government. I was surprised to hear some opposition members, including the last member who has just taken his seat, suggest that we should also endeavour to follow some of the same methods of disposal of our surplus grain as the United States is following.
On a question of privilege, I did not say that. I stressed very clearly that I was not advocating all the methods used by the United States. I made that very clear.
I said some of the methods.

If the hon.
member had heard what I said he would be deliberately misrepresenting.
I repeat that the hon. member suggested that we follow some of the disposal methods followed by the United States.
Some of them.

If the hon. member had
listened to me he would have heard me say that.

The hon.
member did not say that.

I am going to point out to him and to others who raise this same point that there is a great deal of difference between Canada and the United States in this respect. First of all, the population of the United States is over eleven times greater than that of Canada. Second, in the United States they consume right at home 4 bushels of every 5 bushels of wheat they produce. The reverse is true in Canada.

For every 5 bushels we produce we can hardly consume one bushel, and we have to find a market for the other 4 bushels beyond the boundaries of Canada. Wheat is one of our very important export commodities and to suggest that we follow the same methods, that we compete with the United States by selling our wheat for a great deal less or follow its give-away program, is certainly one thing that will wreck the wheat board if it should adopt such a suggestion.
It would mean that either the farmer would get less for his wheat or the taxpayer would have to put up the difference. You can be sure of one thing, that if the taxpayer has to put up the difference between the price that we get on the world market and the price that we would get under such a policy-
Does the hon. member agree with support prices for agriculture? That is what has happened in the United States.
We have price supports and because of our price support program the Canadian farmer is today getting better prices for some of his agricultural products than is the case in the United States.
There is no support price for wheat and the hon. member knows that.
We have a price support program in Canada and we are getting better prices for hogs today than the farmers of the United States.

Let us talk
about wheat. That is what you were talking about and that is what I was talking about.

He does not know that.

speechtext: -and I think I might make the same point again.
He should not talk about me like that, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, despite the very serious problems with which the wheat board is confronted, despite some of the crackpot suggestions we often hear as to what the wheat board should do, the wheat board refuses to be panicked, the wheat board refuses to resort to firesale methods of selling

grain, the wheat board refuses to enter into give-away programs. The wheat board has sold a lot of grain. Last year we had one of the best years in Canadian history so far as sales of wheat are concerned. I think history will record that in that respect the wheat board has done a very excellent job. If it had not been for the wheat board we might be in the same position now as we were in 1932 when the price of wheat went down to the lowest level in Canadian history.
That was the Conservatives. They are through.
There he is again.

We do know that there are powerful interests in this country such as the Winnipeg grain exchange, that would like to dispense with the wheat board system of marketing our grain, but I am not so much concerned about them because we know exactly what they are trying to do. I am more concerned about some of these do-gooders who support the wheat board so vigorously and at the same time make various suggestions which, if adopted by the government or the wheat board, would certainly tend to wreck the board.
That is nonsense.
I say the wheat board has a heavy job. It has a big enough job in handling the problems facing it right now without being saddled with extra responsibility and additional burdens.
Not nearly as tough a job as the farmers.
Another one.

As to the remark made by the hon. member, when it comes to some of the C.C.F. members from Saskatchewan I am not sure who does better in singing the blues, Elvis Presley or my C.C.F. friends from Saskatchewan. Ever since I entered the house in 1949 I have heard nothing from that group but calamity howling, singing of the blues, the country is going to the dogs, depression is just around the corner. I have heard that in the house ever since 1949.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: It went on long before you came here too.

In fact, some of them also do a little rabble rousing on the hustings by suggesting a farmers' march on Ottawa. I understand that the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue)-it is too bad he is not in his seat today-has been urging the farmers to march on Ottawa.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
He is probably out doing it again.

I think that is one of the finest bits of rabble rousing that has taken place in this country. I have before me a Saskatchewan newspaper known as the Yorkton Enterprise. In an editorial they refer to a statement made by a provincial cabinet minister of the C.C.F. government, Mr. Fines.
What date is that?

The date is Thursday, January 31, 1957. This is what the editorial has to say:
Reviewing 1956, Mr. Fines saw it a year of "unparalleled expansion" for Saskatchewan and mentioned three factors he thought responsible.
That is the expansion you said we could not have under a C.C.F. government.

I am quoting Mr. Fines:
"First, a near-record crop, together with better grain marketings, helped farmers recover from the 1954 crop failure and the reduced income level of 1955," he said.
"Second, non-farm production continued its steady and in some cases spectacular development, and contributed almost one-half of total commodity output.
The Winnipeg manifesto did that.

I do not know whether or not they still have the shoe factory there. The quotation continues:
"Third, high levels of public and private investment, including very large inflows from outside the province, made much of this expansion possible."
As I say, listening to what Mr. Fines has to say and listening to my calamity-howling moon-gazing, rabble-rousing C.C.F. friends from Saskatchewan, I do not know whom to believe. Of course, we realize that the farmer has had his difficulties.
The C.C.F. made it difficult for him.
Agriculture has its difficulties. I think that this government recognizes- and it is well known-that agriculture has not fully participated in the increased welfare of our economy in this country.
Who is howling now?

What is the reason for that? 1 can think of no better answer to give than to quote Mr. Hannam when he spoke for the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at the federal-provincial agricultural conference here in Ottawa on December 3 last. This is what he said:
The difficulties in which the farmer today finds himself are basically a result of the fact that not only in Canada but in the whole of the western

Canadian Wheat Board Act world agriculture has been outstandingly successful in increasing productivity and achieving the expansion of production needed to meet post-war food shortages. This increased production represented one of our most urgent post-war needs. The expansion, however, finally outstripped effective market demand for food and agricultural products both at home and abroad. Coupled with this, the world has experienced a lagging behind of farm products in the otherwise notable post-war expansion of trade.
That sounds as though Hannam is howling.

The government has recognized the problems of agriculture. I do not need now to enumerate the benefits extended to the farmers. They include P.F.R.A., P.F.A.A.; price support for our dairy products; price support for our pork; price support for some of the other commodities; the $65 million that was paid under the United Kingdom wheat agreement and others. I was surprised to hear the hon. member who preceded me in speaking in this debate say that this government does not recognize the surpluses problem.
I was only quoting the minister.

Let me remind him that the government assumed the costs incurred by the wheat board in carrying stocks of wheat in excess of normal amount. This is computed on a 15-year average period. On anything over 175 million bushels the government is prepared to pay, with the result that for the 1954-55 pool the taxpayer of Canada has paid the western producer the sum of $31 million, or over 7 j cents per bushel extra to each farmer in western Canada. Does that mean to say that the government does not recognize the surpluses problem? I think it is clear that, under that legislation, the principle of paying the carrying costs on stocks in excess of 175 million bushels is now part of the law of Canada. When carry-overs come back to normal, as some day I hope they will, this legislation will not be valid. But until such time that legislation is on our statute books. I therefore think it is misleading to tell this house that the government is not concerned with regard to these surpluses of wheat in this country.
I was only quoting the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
If you did not have someone to quote, you could not make a speech.
You cannot make one anyway.
Turn up your Hansard and you will see what the government had to say about it.

In spite of the difficult problem that it has to face, I say that the wheat board did an excellent job. A while ago I mentioned the fact that last year we had one of the best selling years for our wheat in the history of this country. We increased our exports to old customers such as the United Kingdom. In the previous year exports to that country amounted to 102 million bushels; last year they amounted to 109 million bushels. To West Germany we increased our exports by 5 million bushels to a figure of 30 million bushels. Exports to Japan remained about the same, namely 29 million bushels. At the same time trade with regard to our wheat was good with countries such as Belgium, Norway, the Netherlands, Ireland and other western European countries. Then we developed or opened up new markets especially with countries behind the iron curtain and were able to sell 45 million bushels of wheat to those countries.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, just before six o'clock I endeavoured to point out that the wheat board system of marketing has many enemies in the country. I also endeavoured to point out that I was not concerned about those who want to get rid of the wheat board system of marketing. They work quite openly, and we know with whom we are dealing, but I am concerned about those do-gooders

and there are some in this house who have spoken in this debate

who profess to be the real friends of the wheat board but who would saddle the board with extra burdens which, if adopted, would certainly tend to wreck the system. I refer to such things as following some of the surplus disposal methods of the United States and the taking of local currency of other countries. If the currency of other countries is as good as Canada's, then of course, there is no problem; but if the currency is not as good as Canada's then, of course, we would have to sell our wheat at a discount, or at next to nothing, and that would mean that the farmer would either get less for his wheat or the taxpayers would have to put up the difference, and certainly that would be one way of wrecking the wheat board.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that the wheat board and the government should refuse to accept some of these so-called fancy deals of accepting local currencies. The farmer would like to see the

fairly high level of prices maintained. The farmer does not want the wheat board to resort to firesale methods, fancy deals or the board get panicky. The farmer would rather sell one bushel of wheat at a fair price and keep the other one at home for the time being than sell his wheat for something less. Therefore, I hope that we do follow the wheat board system of marketing our grain. The farmers in western Canada have fought for this for a number of years. They now have it and they would like to see it maintained. They would like to see the wheat board and the Department of Trade and Commerce continue, as they have in the past, a vigorous campaign of finding new markets for our wheat outside of Canada and, above all, the wheat board maintain the high price level that we have had for our wheat in the past.

Mr. Speaker, the main theme of this debate so far has been, as indicated, the wide acceptance in this house at least of the principle of orderly marketing of our grain. I say "grain" advisedly, Mr. Speaker, because so far we have been hearing a great deal about wheat, which may leave the impression amongst those who are not particularly familiar with the wheat board legislation that it refers to wheat only. I realize that wheat is the most important grain produced in western Canada, but it should not be forgotten that other grains such as oats and barley, rye and flax are also of great importance and in many parts of the prairie provinces are even more important as a grain than wheat itself.
I understand that the orderly marketing principle does in a way open a heartening debate for those of us who believe in orderly marketing of farm products as a principle and as part of our laws. I think it is all the more heartening to hear from members and from party representatives who in the past have not always been quite so friendly to that principle, because basically what has happened in the marketing of grain is that the farmers as well as the consumers have come to the conclusion that this is a commodity which can no longer be left in the hands of private enterprise and which cannot be left to the speculative purposes of those who want to exploit both the consumer and the producer.
The realization of that carries with it a great deal of significance because, as time goes on, it is my guess that that idea will gain ground amongst both the consumers and the producers of this country. In other words, every time that we can show, as I think the wheat board has shown, that it is possible to take an important commodity, and particularly food, out of the realm of speculation,
Canadian Wheat Board Act out of the hands of those who would exploit the producer and the customer and put it into the hands of a board which is there to provide the producer with the best possible return, and to pass on that commodity to the consumer at the most reasonable price in order that the margin in between, or the cost of handling, shall be as inexpensive and as efficiently handled as possible, a great service will be performed.
It is very significant that both the producers and the consumers in Canada, as represented in this house, have come to the conclusion that the least expensive and most efficient manner in which to distribute this very important commodity of Canada, in some respects the most important commodity both in Canada and for export, is to take it out of the realm of private enterprise and put it in the hands of a board responsible to the representatives of both the producer and the consumer.
A great deal has been said about the wheat board itself. When the minister introduced the resolution he made one or two very significant statements to which I wish to refer. First of all, he set out in one paragraph a very important explanation. I am glad he did it because it has given rise to misconceptions in the past. There have been people- and probably there still are-in Canada who were under the impression that in some way the Canadian treasury subsidizes or carries the wheat board. On the other hand, there have been people who have been under the impression-it has included many producers as well-that they have a guaranteed price for their grain. Well, neither one is true. I wish to quote these lines of the minister's explanation which I think bear emphasis. He said, at page 890 of Hansard:
The government authorizes the board to fix an initial price for such wheat as may be delivered to the board within the next crop year, and guarantees the banks against loss through payment of the initial price, but the government does not guarantee payment to the farmer of any price for wheat which is not actually delivered to the board within the crop year.
The reason I repeat these words is to indicate very clearly that the present policy of the government is not to guarantee a price for grain which the farmer produces; it is simply to guarantee the banks against loss of any moneys they advance to the Canadian wheat board for the purposes of the initial price and it is based only on that part of the grain which can actually be delivered. That, of course, depends on the quotas; it depends upon the storage space, availability of box cars, export markets and a great many other factors, so that in effect what the producers have here is only a partial protection so far as the price of the farmer's grain is concerned.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
Then, farther on, the minister said, referring to the recommendations of the Gordon commission:
The Gordon commission recommendations appear to be based upon the assumption that there is likely to be a continuing surplus problem. I do not share that view and I think it would be a great mistake to base our policies on such an assumption.
I agree thoroughly with the last half of the last sentence where the minister says;
... it would be a great mistake to base our policies on such an assumption.
I am not so sure that the minister is quite so right when he says that he does not share the view that we may have a continuing surplus problem.
I will come to that later in my remarks because I believe that is one of the most important matters in connection with the board that we are going to have to face in the next few years; that is, how to devise means by which the Canadian wheat board can continue to provide a service to the producers to an extent which will assure the greatest possible market for their grain.
It has been said that the wheat board has been subject to criticism. I think it would be more correct to say that it has been government policy which has been subject to criticism because the wheat board works within the framework of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. It has only certain powers and certain obligations. It cannot in itself evolve policies which are opposed to the policies held by the government. If the wheat board is going to be rid of a great deal of criticism which does not belong to it, it will be necessary for the government to find ways and means to deal with the surplus position to a greater extent than is envisaged by the minister.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) in his address yesterday gave a little of the historical background of the Canadian wheat board. I found it an extremely interesting review but I also found it to be quite incomplete and I would like to devote just a few minutes to that subject. First of all I think it should be made perfectly clear that the only political party in this house that has consistently and from the very beginning supported the principle of a Canadian wheat board as it is now constituted is the C.C.F. group together with some of the hon. members in the party to my left. I refer to only some of them because it has not been the case with every hon. member in that group.
When the hon. member for Provencher proceeded to describe in rather uncomplimentary terms the policies followed by the Conservative government at the time of

Premier Bennett and the policies advanced by the present Progressive Conservative opposition through their leader, he left a great gap. What he did not state and what I think is important for us to know is that for a great many years, as a matter of fact up until 1943, the policy held by the Liberal party with respect to the wheat board and that held by the Conservative party were almost identical. There was practically no difference whatsoever in their approach. The following remarks were made by the hon. member for Provencher as reported at page 1035 of Hansard for February 6, 1957:
The whole record of what took place in 1935 is available for anybody to see. The question that arises is why would the Conservative government actually enact any legislation at all in 1935 if they did not believe in it? The truth of the matter is that in 1935 the Tories had no sympathy with the compulsory board in the first place, and they tried, apparently as they are trying now, to put the blame for their failure on the opposition.
This seems to me to be a case of the pot calling the kettle black. What was the advice offered by the members of the Liberal party who formed the opposition in 1935? I have here a statement made by the present hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) who was the then hon. member for Macdonald, as it appears on page 3633 of Hansard for June 13, 1935. This was the time when what was known as the grain board was being debated in the house. After having indicated that he would vote for the second reading of the bill in order to get it into committee, the following is the advice that was offered by the hon. member. He said:
At the same time I would hesitate very much to endorse a proposition whereby, at this stage of the game, a permanent compulsory pool organization or board should be established and set in motion to conduct the wheat marketing affairs of the country for years to come. I dislike to see the government go into the grain marketing business.
This was the stand taken not only by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa but also by other hon. members of the opposition of that day including the leader of the opposition, the late Mr. King, when he stated, as will be found on the same page of Hansard, these words:
Especially do we reserve our right to regard this measure as one to deal with a present situation, an emergency situation, and not as necessarily establishing a permanent policy.
As one reads the debate that took place in 1935 one gets the strong impression throughout the record in Hansard that neither the government of the day nor the opposition of the day was at all prepared to accept the principle of orderly marketing of grain through a grain board, or through a wheat board as we refer to it today. Both the government and the official opposition of that

day regarded this as a sort of hasty experiment at that time which was necessary to meet an emergency situation and then to be got rid of as quickly as possible after that.
We are extending it five years now.

Yes, I will come to that in a moment. In his introductory remarks the minister pointed out that in September, 1943 a significant and important change was made in the whole set-up of the Canadian wheat board making it the exclusive marketing agency for all wheat in western Canada. He gave the reason for that change and at page 889 of Hansard for February 1, 1957 stated:
When the open market was below the initial price, producers delivered practically all their wheat to the board. From the point of view of a successful marketing operation by the board, this was a most unsatisfactory position. In a sense it was a sort of "heads I win, tails you lose" proposition.
That is the reason the minister gave for that change. But let me go back to 1935 again and see what sort of advice on that very point was offered by the present hon. member for Portage-Neepawa, the then member for Macdonald. He said, as reported at page 3633 of Hansard:
My feeling at the moment is that if we could establish a grain board which would be in a position to take offers when the market fell below a certain point, and when the market was above that figure for everyone interested in the handling of grain to be free to market in whatever way they saw fit, we would have the most satisfactory arrangement.
Here we have almost the same words used in reverse. Here the spokesman for western Canada of the Liberal opposition of the day said that the most satisfactory situation would be to have the kind of power which would exist only if the price on the open market fell below a certain figure.
We never pretended otherwise.
Do I understand then, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member indicates the policy of the government is still the same?
You are talking about 1935.
Well now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member said they never pretended otherwise and I want to know if the policy of the government remains the same.
Perhaps I may help the hon. member-
Sit down.
Who said sit down?
Someone back there.

I never try to argue that the Liberals in 1935 were not in favour of the
Canadian Wheat Board Act compulsory board. The point I was making is that the Tories now try to pretend they approved of the board in 1935 and they did not. That is my whole point.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the hon. member clear that up. However, I would like to ask the hon. member this question, and if he wishes he can make a reply. Does he at the present time hold the same view as was held by the Liberal party in 1935 with relation to the wheat board?
You know the answer to that one too well to even ask about it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The answer is that the Liberals changed when they crossed the floor.
The answer is in the bill that is before the house. What more do you want?

What happened in September of 1943, Mr. Speaker, which caused this revolution in the thinking of the government of the day? Since 1936 when they came back into power they apparently have been prepared to carry on under the system which had been set out in the quotation I read from the speech made by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa. However, a significant event took place in 1943 which was skipped, and wisely so, in the review made by the hon. member for Provencher. They had made no change up to that time, but in 1943 they did. A most significant thing took place in 1943 which was skipped, as I say, by the hon. member for Provencher. During the summer of 1943, I think it was in August, two by-elections were held in western Canada, one in Selkirk and the other in Humboldt, I believe both on the same day.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Do we have to have this, a discussion of by-elections in 1943? What has this to do with the bill?

It has quite a bit to do with it. I have just referred to the minister's words when he pointed out that the situation was not satisfactory and that it was changed in 1943. This was one of the big issues at that time on the prairies. I remember it very well because I took part in one of those by-elections. The Liberal candidates in both ridings expressed their support of the policy which had been followed up to that time and were completely opposed to the present set-up of the Canadian wheat board. They were quite satisfied to leave it to the open market when it reached a certain price. The farmers expressed themselves very decisively in both ridings, so much so that both the Liberal candidates lost their

Canadian Wheat Board Act deposits and the C.C.F. candidates were elected. Since that time the policy has changed.
I point out that, simply because hon. members on the government side of the house point out that the policy of the official opposition in connection with the wheat board is one of lukewarmness and unreliability. It is quite well to remember that their policy was quite the same until they were forced into a different position. I refer also to the remarks of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre which are reported on page 917 of Hansard of February 1 as follows:
I support with enthusiasm the legislation which is now before us, Mr. Speaker, and 1 want to tell my hon. friends from Saskatchewan on the opposition benches that there are some members in this house who are not keen about the wheat board because they are a little afraid it may be a socialist measure.
It was too bad that when he was speaking the hon. member did not see fit to identify those members who are not so keen about the Canadian wheat board.
If you fellows keep on talking this way you are likely to vote this down.

Hon. members of this house have a right to vote as they please and if they decide to vote this measure down that will defeat the government and we will have an election that much sooner and perhaps a new member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. Since the hon. member has seen fit to interrupt me I would point out that if he is talking in terms of hon. members who are not so keen about the Canadian wheat board because, as he says, it may be a socialist measure, he should identify himself as the first member in that category. There has never been a more reactionary member in this house than the present hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. When he says that he enthusiastically supports this bill I would warn the people in Assiniboia to remember the old saying, "Beware of Greeks bearing gifts." In this case they must beware of a Trojan horse carrying a carpet bag.
Certain recommendations have been made by various farm organizations as to how the present set-up of the wheat board could be improved. One was made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at its annual convention. One recommendation, as reported in the press, was as follows:
The meeting endorsed the Canadian wheat board and the international wheat agreement. A resolution was passed recommending the wheat board be permanently established as the sole marketing agency for all grains produced in western Canada, including flax and rye, and that legislation covering the wheat board be reviewed at regular intervals.
[Mr. Zaplitny.l

That is in line with recommendations that have been made from time to time by members of this group, and again during this debate. We believe that if there is to be orderly marketing the wheat board must be the exclusive marketing agency for grain in western Canada and that it should be a permanent body. We would also include rye and flax in its operations. I find complete unanimity on this point among farm organizations. The Interprovincial Farm Union Council made a presentation to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in December, 1956, which contained this paragraph:
The membership of the Interprovincial Farm Union Council has, on a number of occasions, gone on record as supporting the orderly marketing of wheat, oats and barley, through the facilities of the Canadian wheat board. At the same time, our membership has gone on record equally as often requesting that flax and rye, too, be placed under wheat board jurisdiction. The basis for this request lies in the favourable experience farmers have had in marketing wheat, oats, and barley through board facilities during the past number of years.
Those are recommendations made by the two largest farm bodies in this country which are in perfect identity with the proposals made by members of the C.C.F. group. We ask the government to give them careful consideration and not just slough them aside. If they do not make a move to carry out those recommendations there will be some serious doubts raised in the minds of members of these organizations as to whether best support of the wheat board on the government side is as strong as they pretend it to be.
Some of the other recommendations we have made have to do with the sale of grain and parity prices. I would summarize our recommendations under six headings. First, as I have already said, we feel this should be a permanent statute. Second, it should include rye and flax along with other grains.
Third, we should be prepared to accept the principle of parity prices. If the government will not go so far as to accept that in connection with all grain handled, it should be accepted at least for grain marketed for domestic use. I am using figures produced the other day by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and am assuming they are correct. He indicated that in the United States the parity price for wheat was $2.37. The average price paid for wheat in Canada for the 1954-55 pool, after all deductions for expenses had been made, came to $1.44 per bushel. If you subtract $1.44 from $2.37 you arrive at a differential of 93 cents per bushel.
If we applied that differential to the wheat used in Canada for domestic purposes, and certainly no one who is at all reasonable will deny that there is no reason why wheat or

grain sold in Canada should be sold at a price which is not at parity with the prices of other products, and it is only justice that that be done, it amounts to approximately 70 million bushels of wheat which would come to about $65 million. That means that at the present time the farmers have a perfectly justifiable grievance when they say that the $65 million which could be realized, not by selling their grain at excessive prices but simply at parity prices for domestic use in Canada, should be added to the amount of money in the wheat board fund which could then be distributed in the form of dividends or interim or final payments to the producers. I think that the government or parliament generally should be prepared to go at least as far as to provide that the grain which is sold for domestic consumption would be sold at a price which is considered to be a parity price at the present time.
Then we ask that the government should accept the principle of establishing a national grain reserve. I say a national grain reserve to make it clear that I believe this should be the responsibility of the whole nation, both producers and consumers. If we accept the idea that there should be a reserve of grain we should also accept the principle that this reserve should be maintained and financed as the responsibility of the whole nation and not of the farmers alone. It is a fortunate thing that Canada is in the position of being a great producer of grain with a huge carryover from year to year. It is a fortunate thing for the world, because one never knows when there may be a serious crop failure, or a shortage of food in any corner of the world which will bring people to the point of actual starvation. We are the breadbasket of the world, and if we are to carry out this obligation as a nation, we must not leave it on the shoulders of the producers themselves.
It is not fair to ask the producers of Canada to carry the burden of these huge reserves of grain from year to year. If we accept what I have suggested as a national policy, then we should set up a national food reserve of grain which would be stored and financed by the treasury; the farmers who produce the grain would be paid for the crop they produce and, that having been done, the government would take over. That, in effect, is what is being done in the United States

they are treating the surplus as a national food reserve and then using various means to market that grain both on the domestic market and in countries abroad.
This brings me to the fifth point. We propose that the government should seriously explore ways of obtaining new revenues and export markets. I know that the minister
Canadian Wheat Board Act and some of the hon. members on the other side of the house have stated, even in their speeches during this debate, that these methods used by the United States to dispose of its grain were open to question. They have called it a "fire sale".
A "give-away".

That is another description which the hon. member has supplied. I think it is a little shortsighted to approach a well-thought-out program which has proved to be effective and beneficial to the nation and to the producers in the United States, with such an attitude, and to laugh it off as a fire sale or as a give-away. As a matter of fact it is neither one thing nor the other.
It certainly is.

If the hon. member for
Moose Jaw-Lake Centre would take the trouble to inform himself of what is actually being done in the United States with regard to the disposal of grain I am sure he would not use those terms. They have a number of ways, in the United States, of applying this plan which I have mentioned, but I will refer only to three of them. One of the ways is by selling grain for local currencies- various currencies.
That is the Mutual Security Act.
It is giving it away.
No, not at all. It is accepting local currencies for the purpose of being able to make a deal which would not otherwise be possible.
What do you do with the local currency?

Part of it is held to the credit of the exporting nation to be liquidated by goods to be obtained from the country to which the grain has been delivered.
The other method used to dispose of the grain is intended to promote the expansion and development of the countries concerned-*
Britain won't buy it that way.

It is a desirable way in which to carry on trade with these countries. One can call it a give-away or a fire sale, but I think it is a smart way to do business, and since it is the only way in which you can do business with these countries I think it is smart to take advantage of the opportunity.
No.

You have not made one suggestion as to how we could sell more wheat.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
