I have never objected to
interruptions. I rather enjoy them, and sometimes I make them myself, but I would appreciate it if only one member at a time would interrupt so that I could identify who is speaking and reply to what they say.
The other method used is what they describe as disaster or famine relief. That could be called, in some sense, a give-away but the amount so disposed of represents only a very small part of the total grain dealt with under this project.
Another method by which they dispose of a great amount of their grain is in exchange for strategic materials, either from the country to which the grain is shipped or from some other country with which the country of the first part may have a credit. What does all this amount to? I want to point out to hon. members that this is no laughing matter. In the crop year of 1955-56 they have disposed of 156.3 million bushels for local currencies.
Gave it away.
At substantial discounts.

Using the second method I have described, they disposed of 67.4 million bushels in one phase and 112 million bushels under a slightly different plan. If you limit the figure for famine relief-it is not given, but it can be estimated-to 10 million bushels, you will find they have disposed of a total of 335 million bushels of grain through the commodity grain corporation.

We exported 309 million
bushels for cash.

Yes, but these 335 million bushels of grain was over and above what they sold for cash-it is over and above what the United States sold in the course of regular commercial transactions. The hon. member says we have sold about that much for cash, but they have sold by special deals as much as we have sold for cash through these various deals, plus what they have sold in the course of their various commercial transactions.
If my hon. friends do not think that this deserves at least an intelligent investigation -that it does not deserve at least the courtesy of study and consideration on behalf of the producers of Canada, and can simply be laughed off-that would indicate to me that they are not particularly anxious to improve our export situation. And let me say this-
We are going to vote for this bill despite you.

We are going to be faced for years with these surpluses. The pressure is going to become greater and greater on this parliament, and consequently on the wheat board, to find ways and means of improving our export position and I think the least we can do is to give intelligent and serious consideration to these means which I have referred to, and apply that part of the plan which is applicable to Canada under Canadian conditions. If we do that, we shall have done something.
I see my time is rapidly running out. As my last point, I would say this. We have asked, and we ask again, that a system of cash advances for grain be instituted so that the farmers may be put into a position of carrying on their normal operations. We cannot expect them to do this unless we provide some system of cash advances so that farmers can at least get the money required to undertake their normal expenditure.
I thank the Chair for the courtesy it has shown me. I see my time is a little overdue, but I imagine some time has been added on account of interruptions.

Before the hon. member takes his seat, I wonder whether he would answer a question. I dislike guilt by association without the naming of the people who might not support the wheat board. Would the hon. member please indicate whom in the Social Credit party he meant who might not support the wheat board?

I do not think I said there were any members to my left who did not support the wheat board as such. What I did say was that not all members of the group regard the wheat board in exactly the same way, and that is indicated by their own speeches. Unfortunately I do not have time to go into the record now to show that but I think I have indicated quite truthfully that not all members of the party to my left regard the wheat board in exactly the same light.
Mr. Speaker, I rather regret to see a tendency to inject unnecessary politics in a discussion of the wheat board.
Far be it from you.

It is far too difficult a problem to arrive at a solution of to indulge in such lightmindedness as playing politics concerning the very important matter of the production, conservation and marketing of wheat. In commencing my remarks I should like to refer to the submission of the Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation to the royal commission on Canada's economic

prospects in a 43 page brief that they submitted in the fall of 1955. In short, the general message of their submission was that a continuation of recent trends would spell disaster for agriculture.
It is well to bear in mind who it was who made the submission and to whom they were making it and then reflect that these people solemnly declare that unless the trends in agriculture now in progress in Canada are changed the whole set-up spells disaster for Canadian agriculture. That is not calamity howling. That is the serious, sober message of the Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation in the fall of 1955.
I do not propose to go into any considerable detail with respect to what these people had to say but I will quote one short passage from their 43 page brief. This one has to do with the loans which are necessary in order that our farmers may be able to carry on. It reads:
We are forced to the conclusion that government backing for agriculture loans is essential, and for the maximum diversification and wider spreading of the risks, this must be a nationwide scheme sponsored by the federal government. We favour increased use of Canadian farm loan board facilities with interest rates at the lowest level possible.
I hasten to concede that the Liberal government has gone a considerable distance in the direction of meeting the demands of that statement but I am sure that every hon. member who has given the matter any sober thought is convinced that the federal government has not gone far enough yet. That is all I propose to say in introducing what I wish to talk about tonight.
I wish to say that the Social Credit case with regard to wheat has been put by the hon. members for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smith) and Bow River (Mr. Johnston).
And New Westminster.

I believe that in a general way they have put the whole case completely. They have not done so, of course, in every detail but I support wholeheartedly the cases put forward by these three members, and all Social Crediters will be prepared to do the same with respect to the wheat growers of the prairie provinces. We will grant that the British Columbia members have a problem which was very well indicated by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) the other day. In my judgment that problem has to be met and dealt with. But the Social Credit program, as the three members whom I have mentioned have outlined, has to do particularly with the well-being of the wheat grower on the prairie farms.
In the first place, we approve of the wheat board. We will all vote for the wheat board.
Canadian Wheat Board Act I am sure we all have voted for the wheat board and we have voted for the wheat board without all the frills which I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) tried very hard to imply that we wanted, to add to the responsibilities of the board with the danger of wrecking the wheat board. I think it was quite unworthy of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make those remarks. He is old enough to know better. I will have something to say about that later.
As I said, we favour the wheat board as the means of marketing wheat, oats and barley and we desire that flax and rye shall be added to the commodities marketed through the wheat board.
We favour advances on farm-stored grain and here, of course, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) and others who are looking for us to bring up something like this, including the Minister of Trade and Commerce, will begin to writhe. But let me specify that these advances on farm-stored grain are to be made directly from a federal agency outside the wheat board entirely. There is no reason why government money cannot be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada directly, without having the wheat board assume any responsibility with respect to either administration or to the provision of the means of paying. Certainly everyone with a tithe of the experience of the Minister of Trade and Commerce ought to know that. These advances on farm-stored grain would be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
The old taxpayer.

Yes, of course, the whole taxpayer, just as the whole taxpayer pajs for all they are doing in the United States. If, with the tremendous potential production of the United States, that country with its enormous population finds it wise to pay for the well-being of their farmers, I think we will find that Canada can afford to do the same kind of thing. Here we have France giving special considerations and even Turkey and many other countries economically far inferior to Canada in every possible way. Yet they are able to make payments out of their consolidated revenue funds of money paid by all the taxpayers, just as the taxpayers in the three prairie provinces are contributing generously to the provision of funds with which to pay for a great many other expenses incident to the carrying on of the life of Canada at the present time.

Including the
seaway.

As my hon. friend has said, including the seaway, and many other

Canadian Wheat Board Act projects. We are not complaining, and it is high time that the ordinary taxpayer of Canada stopped complaining about trying to help us out in our time of need. That is important to bear in mind. If we cannot face this problem as solid, sober Canadians, what is the use of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) talking about unity in Canada? What does unity in Canada mean if it does not mean united we stand and divided we fall with reference to every aspect of our economy and the carrying on of our national life?
The government already has an example of what can be done and the government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce know that it can be done. The government has already agreed to pay storage on all grain in excess of 178 million bushels. Where is the money going to come from? From the wheat board? No, it is going to come from the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. Why cannot the same source be used for the money with which to pay advances on farm-stored grain?
Take it all, John.
We only get what you fellows leave.

That is the second thing. Now for the third one, and this is an exceedingly important matter. It is that we make provision for adequate, approved storage facilities on the farms and that that provision shall also be made out of the consolidated revenue fund and not through the wheat board. We do not expect the wheat board to build the great terminal elevators the government build. We do not expect the wheat board to build the elevators all over the land including the pool elevators that are built. They are built by other agencies. Approved farm storage, which in my judgment ought to be on every farm in Canada where the farmer so desires it, ought to be built through a fund which will not be a responsibility of the wheat board but which will come either directly out of the Bank of Canada or out of the consolidated revenue of Canada, whichever one the government sees fit to use.
This matter of approved farm storage is exceedingly important for several reasons. I think nearly everyone who has given careful thought to the agricultural problems of Canada, as have most of the hon. members in this chamber in all parties, realizes that the time is coming before long when many of the storage facilities which we now have, like pool elevators and the various line elevators, will have to be renewed. They are wearing out. Already the interest on the

capital invested in those facilities is so heavy that it raises the cost of storage to the farmer so high that it is almost crushing him. When those facilities come to be rebuilt, unless some most unforeseen thing occurs, they will be rebuilt at costs at least three times as great as were the costs when they were first built, and the interest on all that capital expenditure will be added to the burden which now rests on the farmer, in the matter of storage of his grain, as another additional crushing weight to squeeze out what little bit of economic life there still is in him.
We cannot afford to disregard these matters. If we can get approved farm storage built on the farm and so manage that the farmer himself comes to own those storage facilities, then we shall be on the way toward a situation in which we can overcome much of this onerous burden of interest which now is resting so heavily upon our farmers. I therefore repeat that we want approved farm storage on the farm wherever the farmer so desires.
We want parity prices on grains. Of course that involves subsidies. Let not the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) nor any of his cohorts rise and say that there is another proposal that will wreck the wheat board. It will do nothing of the sort. The money which will pay those subsidies to produce parity prices will come once more out of the consolidated revenue fund; yes, it will come out of the taxpayers just as those special subsidies which pay high prices for the grain produced in England-little England burdened and beset with all manner of trouble -come out of the taxpayers. The taxpayers are glad to pay those subsidies.
Oh, oh.

Yes, they are. Every taxpayer that is informed and not deluded by a lot of silly socialism is glad to pay. Every taxpayer realizes that every bushel of wheat that can be produced in Britain is one more step in guaranteeing that he will be able to eat in time of sore trial, and that is no small consideration. He has been through it twice. He has been through two times of sore trial when he was not more than about two weeks from starvation: in world war I and in world war II. Do not imagine that he wants to be in such danger again. I therefore do not hesitate to suggest that the general taxpayer in Canada should pay in order to subsidize so as to give the farmers a fair price.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) pointed out that when the manufacturers in Canada of machines that the farmers must have take it into their heads that they will advance the price of machines six per cent- as they did two years ago-they do not ask

the government for permission to do so-or if they do so, it is all behind the scenes-but they advance that price, and what do they do? They take it out of the taxpayers of Canada just as easily as falling off a log and the general taxpayers of Canada pay.
They pay money in higher wages.

They pay in all sorts of ways. When the price of steel was advanced in 1946, with the direct consent of the government and maybe of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, by $5 a ton, did the Canadian people as a whole have anything to say about it? Not a word. It was just done, and the cost of producing all over Canada was raised by an enormous amount just by that simple move that those people made, just as simply as a raindrop would fall from heaven. The Canadian taxpayers paid it directly and indirectly, and they are still paying it. Then the steel workers struck and remained on strike for 82 days in order to get their share of the $5 a ton. They finally got their increase in wages and the increase in wages finally went across all Canada and everybody in Canada paid it-* every taxpayer-and is still paying it.
We must be realistic in approaching all these matters. Hence I say we want parity prices. We want the subsidies to be paid out of government revenue and not by the wheat board. Social Credit advocates a parity price of $2.37 per bushel for domestic market wheat and we want a fair price on the wheat that is sold abroad. I do not propose to go into any detail with regard to that matter at the present time.
We in my constituency and we Social Crediters as a whole approve the present international wheat agreement. We do not feel that the price was high enough but we believe in international wheat agreements. We approve of the one which has already been negotiated and under which we have been carrying on for some time now.
In my constituency, and generally throughout the prairie provinces, there is great dissatisfaction with the allocation of box cars at the present time. The blame for this situation is not to be laid at the door of the wheat board as many hon. members, including the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore), truthfully pointed out. Of course it is none of the Wheat Board's business. They are not charged with the responsibility of providing box cars. Just what are all the reasons behind the difficulties from which we have suffered for several years now in respect of box cars it would perhaps take almost a royal commission to determine because there is a great deal of disagreement
Canadian Wheat Board Act concerning the matter.	But nevertheless,
whoever is responsible for seeing that those box cars get out there so that the farmer can sell to the elevator of his choice, he should be getting into action and producing results at the earliest possible time; and we are so demanding through this speech that I have now been giving, or at least my constituency is doing so.
We insist on the maintenance of the Crows-nest pass agreement	undisturbed and
unaltered. We hear so much talk about a proposed modification of that Crowsnest pass agreement that it makes us furious every time we think about it. We do not want a change even to be thought of.
That is all I propose to say at the present time in a general way in supplement of what has already been said by the three members whom I have mentioned as being spokesmen for the Social Credit position.
Before taking my seat I wish to say that there is a good deal of debating among farmers in my constituency who are affected. There are some of them who speak through the interprovincial farm union, and some of them who speak through the Alberta wheat pool. There are others who speak through the Canadian federation of agriculture, I suppose. Before I take my seat I propose to read the proposals that have been made by the Alberta wheat pool delegates during the past year. I am reading from the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of January 18, 1957, at page 2:
A number of policy resolutions were passed at the 34th annual meeting of the Alberta wheat pool delegates which indicate their stand on many matters pertaining to grain marketing. In most cases they were re-endorsements of previous policy. They were:
1.	Support of the Canadian wheat hoard as the sole marketing agency for western Canada grain and expression of appreciation of the present operations.
2.	Renewal of pressure to have flax and rye marketed by the Canadian wheat board made even more urgent since both grains are on quota.
3.	Approval of the present international wheat agreement.
4.	Commendation of the government's action in concluding wheat deals with iron curtain countries in line with requests from wheat pool delegates, last year, "that aggressive sales policies be adopted in all countries, including those behind the iron curtain," and recommendations that this market be further developed.
5.	Approval of the government's undertaking to assume carrying charges on part of the surplus wheat stocks, this being partial fulfilment of last year's request from the delegate body.
6.	The recommendation of a domestic price for wheat of $2 a bushel, the ceiling of the present international wheat agreement.
7.	A reinstatement of their insistence that the Crowsnest pass agreement must not be disturbed or altered.
8.	Instructions to the board of directors to continue, with every means possible, the campaign to have box cars allocated to elevators on the basis of the farmer's choice.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
9.	Urge that the government offer inducement to farmers to take land out of wheat acreage and plant it to a soil-building crop. They suggested that a representative committee of governments and farm organizations be set up to draw up a plan.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the end of my contribution to the discussion of wheat thus far in the year 1957.

speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is rising to take part in the debate?

Mr. Speaker, I did feel that I would like to say a few words in the debate. The house will realize that I do not profess to be any authority upon the matter of the wheat board; but as I listened to the genial member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) speak this afternoon I must confess that I found myself rather puzzled at the way in which the members of the Social Credit group, including the hon. member for Bow River, appear to be able to speak out of both sides of their mouths at the same time.
Having listened to a number of speakers on the subject of wheat marketing in this house, I recognized that there was some similarity in some of the things which the hon. member for Bow River was saying to some of the arguments which are advanced by the members of the C.C.F. group in this house with respect to wheat policy and the wheat board. I am quite sure that the hon. member for Bow River, and the other members of his party who have spoken in support of second reading of this bill, were quite sincere in putting forward the views that they have expressed.
Thank you for the compliment.
But the thing that puzzles me is the rather neat way in which they are able to keep their thinking in separate compartments in relation to different aspects of the life of the Canadian people.
If you had one compartment you would be lucky.

I recall that some little time ago I listened to a speech delivered in this house by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). It seems to me that if the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Macleod were consistent the sentiments expressed on that occasion by the hon. member for Macleod would be the sort of things that one would expect to hear him and the hon. member for Bow River say in relation

to the passage or otherwise of the bill that is now before us. I am referring to a speech which the hon. member for Macleod made in 1955, which will be found at page 314 of Hansard of that year. On that occasion he was making some comments on the policies of the Liberal party and of the C.C.F. party, and he was suggesting that the Liberal party in some ways was just a little smarter than the C.C.F. party.
Oh, oh.
Read on.

I am sure that the house might be interested in being reminded of some of the ensuing remarks and interjections that were made in the house on that occasion, but I think I have read enough of the speech of the hon. member for Macleod to illustrate the point I have in mind.
As I understand the idea behind the Canadian wheat board, it is to establish, under the responsibility of the government of Canada, an agency for the orderly marketing of Canadian grain. There may be some other aspects to it that I have not yet been able to comprehend, but essentially that is what I understand it to be. That is why I am surprised that people like the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Macleod on other occasions-we will just say simply the members of the Social Credit party-

You are not
right in either instance. The remarks you have just read have nothing to do with the wheat board.

That is why I am surprised that when they come to a discussion of having the government handle and look after the farmer's grain in the province of Alberta they are prepared to go along and support the ideas that are supported by people they call socialists in this house.
Heaven forbid!

As far as any other aspect of our Canadian life is concerned, they are perfectly prepared to throw the rest of the Canadian people to the wolves of what they call free enterprise. I think it is about time they began to straighten out their thinking on some of these matters. It is all very well for them to come to this house and set themselves up as a little farm pressure group representing the interests of a certain group of farmers in one province of this country. They may think it is all right for them to do that on the one hand, but when it comes to supporting any other constructive proposal which involves action through the medium of the government of Canada, then they of course are quite loud in their declamations of their adherence to the principle of free enterprise.
Are you talking about the wheat board?
He would not know.
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking in support of the bill that is before the house.
Hear, hear.
Which bill is it?
I support the views being put forward by hon. members of the C.C.F. group who represent grain growing areas of Canada.
They don't all do that. What about the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge)? He doesn't.

One of the reasons I am in full support of the policies they have been advocating is that I know they are doing so not simply as a little pressure group from a certain segment of the country but because they believe this is the kind of legislation that will contribute to the welfare of the Canadian people and are prepared to support the application of similar principles in respect of other economic and geographic regions of the country.
Earlier this evening an article came to my attention which is to be found at page 19 of the Vancouver Province of Monday, February 4.
In connection with the wheat board?

It is entitled, "Why lumbermen grind their teeth". Among other things the article sets forth that British Columbia lumber exports in 1956 dropped by 371,034,908 board feet over 1955, from 1,016,824,698 to 645,789,790. Domestic shipments fell by 51,363,570 board feet in the same period from 395,234,257 to 343,870,687.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
He is talking sawdust now.
Is that first grade lumber or second?
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that the wording of the present bill should be changed to read "The Canadian, wheat and lumber board".
What would be wrong with that?

However, I wonder what the attitude of my Social Credit friends would be if the situation should develop in the lumber export business of British Columbia where some sort of approach by the government of Canada, perhaps somewhat in the same direction as has been made in respect of the marketing of wheat, were required to ensure the continued and stable marketing of the lumber products of British Columbia.
You have that in Saskatchewan and we don't want it.
Do not forget to mention fish, too.

I think the house should be entitled to some more balanced expression of the views of the Social Credit party as to why they are prepared to endorse this particular kind of legislation if they propose a similar move in a field other than the one under discussion.
We would be satisfied to-have even one balanced expression from the C.C.F. party.
Carried.

I think perhaps some hon. members of the Social Credit group who have what I believe is a genuine concern for the welfare of the farming population of Alberta should look a little deeper into their relationship with the political thinking of the people who go under the same political label in the neighbouring province of British Columbia. I am somewhat afraid that before too long they are going to find it increasingly difficult to reconcile the proposal they are now supporting with the general policies that are being advanced in many quarters within the same political group.

Mr. Speaker, it occurs to me that it must be obvious to-the house that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), who has just finished speaking, does not know too much about wheat. I think it is obvious to all that he should have stuck strictly to-

Nuts.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

-the field where he is probably better informed, namely that of fishing. Some of the extracts from Hansard which he endeavoured to tie in with this debate were probably just as unrelated to the facts before us as was his reference to lumber.
In spite of the fact that several hon. members of the C.C.F. party have striven to create the impression that we in this group are not in support of the Canadian wheat board as the sole marketing agency of wheat I wish to underline what should be known to all hon. members, namely that throughout this debate and throughout the years gone by we have supported the Canadian wheat board as the sole marketing agency for Canadian wheat, and no attempt on the part of socialist members can create an impression that is otherwise.
My purpose in rising, Mr. Speaker, is to make specific reference to only one matter, the position of transport controller. This is an aspect of the whole matter of the Canadian wheat board and wheat marketing that is of particular concern to us. I listened with interest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he referred to the position of the transport controller as being completely untenable. I have thought about that expression very frequently since the minister made the statement and I would ask if in the course of closing this debate he would elaborate upon the statement he made on February 1. Does he mean that the transport controller has found through his experience he cannot face the members of the Canadian House of Commons in the agriculture committee?

He cannot meet their
requirements.

If I may use the term, I would say that describing the position of transport controller as untenable is completely unflattering. Is it a reflection upon the courage of qualified Canadians who, if asked, might accept the appointment? I ask the minister to let this house know if anyone has been approached and offered the appointment of transport controller since Mr. Milner's resignation became effective December 31. We know that the position of transport controller must be a difficult one.
It is.
He is caught between the wheat board, the farmers, the railways and-
The C.C.F.

-government policy. I would like to know if these conflicts were actually reflected in the questions that were asked by hon. members in the agriculture committee and if it was those questions which did in fact cause the transport controller to resign.

It seems to me there must be something deeper involved in this than we have yet learned. It is not the first time that an official has been called before a committee of this house and subjected to rather severe crossexamination, but we find very few officials resigning as a consequence of that. Was Mr. Milner dissatisfied with government policy? Did he find inadequate the powers granted to him as transport controller by this government?
We feel we should have an answer to that question. Did he resign to take another position such as the chairmanship of the board of grain commissioners? The minister has said that the position is completely untenable. Is he suggesting that the position of controller and action taken by the controller should be beyond the criticism of the agriculture committee of the House of Commons? I would ask the minister finally to tell us once and for all whether he considered the position of transport controller necessary? Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce, does the Department of Agriculture, does the government as a whole actually consider the position of transport controller necessary?
At this stage we have reason to believe that such an appointment is necessary. The minister has said the position is untenable. We do not know whether anyone has been approached. As far as I am concerned personally I am quite in the dark with respect to this whole thing.
I am hoping the minister will deal in detail with these things. Before sitting down may I emphasize again that we have supported the Canadian Wheat Board Act and the Canadian wheat board as the sole marketing agency, but that does not mean that at all times and under all circumstances we agree with the prices being paid for farm grains. We do recognize that it has brought a degree of orderliness into the marketing of these farm products.
I rose principally to ask these questions with respect to the transport controller and t think before we pass this bill we should be given the answers.

speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member for Kindersley is on his feet and wishes to speak?

Mr. Speaker, I was on my feet when the minister rose. I am pleased to take part in this debate and I was waiting to see if other government members from Saskatchewan would display their enthusiasm for the principle of orderly marketing. It is apparent however that their interest in this matter is limited indeed.
I am pleased to take part in this debate because it gives us in this group an opportunity to try to convince members from all parts of Canada of the desirability of maintaining the system of orderly marketing which we have finally achieved through the Canadian wheat board. This is an example of what can be done by government planning. It is in marked contrast with the system which the government allowed to prevail before the introduction of a compulsory board. The system of marketing under the Winnipeg grain exchange was indeed chaotic and left the individual farmer to the mercy of the speculators and the returns he received for his product bore little or no relation to the cost of production. The returns we get from our wheat still bear no relation to the cost of production, but one result of this system of orderly marketing has been a stabilizing of prices so the farmer may know within the crop year what price he can expect to receive for his products.
I wish members of the government were as forthright in their request for orderly marketing schemes as the C.C.F. have been. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), this has been a C.C.F. policy since its inception. We have heard some idiotic remarks to the effect that the C.C.F. are attempting to sabotage the wheat board. If there is anyone in the house who can document that statement, who can give a quotation from Hansard indicating a statement of policy by the C.C.F. against the principle of orderly marketing by the Canadian wheat board, I would be only too pleased to have him put it on the record.
If the government were honestly convinced that this principle of orderly marketing was desirable I would expect that they would attempt to encourage it in other fields. I submit that the principle of orderly marketing which we have achieved for our grain could be extended to livestock, but I have noticed on past occasions when members of this party have attempted to have the orderly marketing principle extended to livestock we were vigorously and vehemently opposed by the government, the so-called champions of this system of orderly marketing.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
They could have brought in provisions for a poultry marketing board which would have taken care of the serious and violent fluctuations in poultry prices which presently exist and which are apparently beyond the capabilities of this government to resolve.
If this government was dedicated to maintaining this principle of orderly marketing it certainly would have included flax and rye and thus extinguished for all time the Winnipeg grain exchange which has preyed on the farmers of Canada for the past number of years.
Indeed, if the government was honestly interested in maintaining this system of orderly marketing it would carry out the suggestion made by all speakers in this party and make the legislation permanent. It would put it on the statute books of Canada so that we would not run the risk of some future government which was not in favour of this principle of orderly marketing taking it off the statute books.
The system of orderly marketing which we have under the Canadian wheat board is able to operate only within the legal terms defined by this government. Its operations are continually complicated by the barriers which this government puts up to confound it. I think we can well imagine the ease with which the Canadian wheat board could operate under the administration of a government which believed in economic planning for the benefit of all rather than a privileged few. We find that the only political party in this house which believes in organizing our economy for the benefit of all rather than for the privilege of a few is the party to which I belong.
It has been stated that one of the reasons- indeed the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has said it is the sole reason- for our large carryover is the series of bumper crops we have had in western Canada. Only recently be made reference to the decline in wheat acreage which has occurred, but he did not take any credit for that. I would point out to the minister that that decline came about because farmers have been forced out of the production of wheat. Many of those farmers have land suited to the growing of wheat and since we have achieved a system of orderly marketing through the Canadian wheat board for our wheat it is only natural that they will tend to follow that production which has reasonable security.
How much better it would be, and how much simpler it would be for the Canadian wheat board, if we had a government agricultural policy which would give the same stability and security to farmers who are

Canadian Wheat Board Act raising livestock, poultry, and other grains. If we had an indication of what prices we could expect in the future, we would then be in a position to plan our production. The dominion-provincial agricultural conference specifically has this function. But, Mr. Speaker, this conference meets each year; the members carefully divulge their platitudes to each other, the federal government, under the leadership of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), supplies various quantities of figures to prove various contentions, and the net result is a complete lack of guidance to the farmers of western Canada. The Interprovincial Farm Union Council has suggested and requested that this conference should make some concrete proposals to guide farmers in their future activities.
I think this could also apply to other aspects of government policy. We experience these bumber crops, and we have the largest carry-over of wheat on record. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) put on record some of the solutions which have been offered by this party, but I would like to point out again that the wheat board is only as effective in disposing of this grain as government trading policies will allow it to be. If our trade policies are continually geared to a deficit, how can we expect to sell wheat on a very competitive market in anything above the present quantities.
These are some of the barriers which this government is putting in the way of orderly marketing by the Canadian wheat board. They have, moreover, refused, in the face of demands from farm organizations of western Canada, to introduce a system of cash advances to allow individual farmers to have some return with which to operate their farms. We went over the subject very thoroughly last year when the government proposed its bank loan legislation-legislation which has been a complete and unequivocal failure. It has been a failure because it does not supply the needs of the farmers.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated that the wheat board should not operate a system of cash advances. I think he has assumed we are requesting that the present officials of the Canadian wheat board should assume this responsibility; but he will be the first to admit, from his experience of the operations of the Canadian wheat board, that a system of cash advances must be operated in very close co-operation with the wheat board, and be an agency of government established in conjunction with it.
The purpose of this proposal is, of course, to allow farmers from different areas to have the same opportunity to get a return from their grain. It is most unfair for a farmer in
[Mr Johnson (Kindersley).]

one area to have a four-bushel or five-bushel quota when a farmer not many miles away has a unit or a one-bushel quota. The purpose of a cash advance is to equalize these returns. If a man is denied the privilege of delivering his grain to the elevator, he should have the privilege of receiving the same money for that grain as if he had a box car available to deliver it.
While I am dealing with this subject of box cars and quotas, I should deal for a moment with the largest barrier that this government has set up in the way of the Canadian wheat board. The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated in his opening remarks that the Canadian wheat board is a marketing agency. I would agree with that definition. But I would ask the minister why they have saddled the Canadian wheat board with the onerous responsibility of distributing box cars. They have saddled the board with this responsibility because of their dismal failure with regard to appointing a man as transport controller to ensure that cars are distributed. I recall that last year, when we were discussing the bill to extend the powers of the transport controller, it was indicated that the responsibility of the Canadian wheat board was to allocate shipping orders, but that the responsibility of seeing box cars were available to fill those orders rested with the transport controller-the more arduous task of the two, perhaps.
Yet now we have this post left vacant since the former transport controller, Mr. Milner, moved on to a higher position with the board of grain commissioners. Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is a very satisfactory situation to find the government hiding behind the criticism which has been directed at the former transport controller in justification for its refusal to appoint a new transport controller. It is apparent that the resignation of the former transport controller was prompted by the differences of opinion which he had with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I vividly recall the meetings of the agriculture committee when the C.P.R. gave its evidence before the members of that committee. The failure of the government to appoint a transport controller to direct the movements of box cars along these railway lines to marketing points is an indication of the complete submission of this government to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
There is evidence, Mr. Speaker, that the situation is not as rosy as many members on the government benches would have us believe as far as the quota position is concerned. The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated last year that preference would be given to those points which were unable to deliver the same quota as other points, which indicated

that at the end of the last crop year some farmers would be able to deliver seven bushels an acre, and others would be confined to four or five bushels to the acre. They used as an excuse for that the desirability of getting the class and kind of grain required into position. They needed that excuse because the transport controller was not using his powers-or, should I say, the government was not seeing that the transport controller used his powers to ensure an equitable distribution of boxcars.
I had a resolution sent to me from the Hazlet branch of the Canadian Legion which is an accurate interpretation of much of the thinking of farmers at these low marketing points, and since it is very short, I would like to place it on the record. It is a resolution passed unanimously at a meeting of branch No. 202 on January 10:
Whereas the Minister of Trade and Commerce the Hon. C. D. Howe stated at the close of the 1955-56 crop year that points on low quotas at that time would be given priority for quotas and boxcars in the new crop year and-
Whereas the quota at the close of the 1955-56 crop year was five bushels per seeded acre at Roseray and six bushels per seeded acre at Hazlet, and
Whereas the quota on January 10, 1957, is one bushel per seeded acre at Roseray and two bushels per seeded acre at Hazlet we resolve thatquotas be increased and boxcars allocated to these points immediately to bring deliveries up to a par with stations which had seven to eight bushel quotas at the close of the last crop year, many of which are on a three to four bushel quota at this time.
Mr. Speaker, when we have a situation like this occurring in the country, who gets the blame? The person who gets the blame is the person saddled with this responsibility, and some criticism is directed at the Canadian wheat board because of the boxcar distribution-through the failure of this government to appoint a controller to take this heavy burden of responsibility from the shoulders of the Canadian wheat board.
I have given indication of the stand of this party with respect to the system of orderly marketing. I have given some indication of the obstacles the government is continually placing in the way of a continuation of the system of orderly marketing. I say to the minister and the other members of the government that action must be taken to make the Canadian Wheat Board Act permanent legislation and to include rye and flax under the operations of the board so that in spite of the indifference of the government we will have a complete example of how orderly marketing can be effective in the Canadian economy.
I should like the government to give consideration to extending the system of orderly marketing to the other fields I have enumerated. As we proceed with such a program 82715-69J
Canadian Wheat Board Act in conjunction with a sensible over-all agricultural policy I think we will achieve some measure of relief to lift the farmers out of the cost-price squeeze in which they find themselves today. The problem is increasingly serious. Farmers become critical of the supply of box cars. They become critical of the quotas because of the pressure put on them as the result of their limited deliveries.
Government policy in allowing inflation to run away and in allowing the cost of production to rise is just as responsible for any discontent existing among the farmers as limited deliveries. If the prices of goods and services had been maintained at a proper level I think the farmers would be able to operate on a quota of seven or eight bushels an acre. At least they would have been able to survive. As it is now, with limited quotas and severe inflation in all aspects of our economy, it is most difficult for them to make ends meet with limited deliveries and the low prices they receive.
My colleagues have placed on the record other aspects of C.C.F. policy in connection with the orderly marketing of our grain. I do not think I need to repeat them now but I will look forward to hearing the minister state the attitude of the government with respect to the early appointment of a transport controller, making the wheat board legislation permanent and the inclusion of flax and rye under the operations of the board.
You still have not told us how to sell more wheat.

Mr. Speaker, before the debate concludes I should like to say a word because I come from a wheatgrowing section of the country. I have also attended a good many farmers' meetings, have carried on a good deal of correspondence with respect to wheat-growing problems and have received numerous resolutions from time to time. The bill now before us gives us an opportunity to speak about the operations of the Canadian wheat board and to say whether or not we are in favour of the continued life of the board.
I am quite certain that the wheat-growing farmers of Canada are almost unanimous in their desire to have the Canadian wheat board continued. Wherever I go I find that this desire exists. There is the odd occasion when some may say that they wish we could go back to the type of wheat marketing we had before the board took over all deliveries of wheat.
I recall being at a farmers' meeting a number of years ago. They had their problems. Among their problems was that of

Canadian Wheat Board Act marketing their grain as well as the price they were receiving at that particular time. The chairman of the meeting was the reeve of the municipality and it happened that the reeve was a very good political supporter of mine. I do not know whether or not I made any remarks which left a wrong impression. I think perhaps I did try to explain that there was another side to the question of marketing wheat which the odd individual may have expressed. However, no matter what remarks I may have made at the time, after the meeting the reeve came to me and in spite of the fact that he was a very good supporter of mine he said "Mr. Hansell, we are glad to know that you support the wheat board but if you ever talk against it in the House of Commons there will be no use of your ever coming into this community again." That was said by a man who knew what he was talking about and I think he was only expressing the opinion of almost 100 per cent of the farmers of that community.
I believe that the reason the farmers want the continuation of the wheat board is that it does tend towards a more orderly marketing policy. The farmer is not left altogether to chance. Not only does it offer a more orderly marketing policy but it puts the farmer in a position where he is a little more certain of his future. He is not dependent upon fluctuations which might occur on the open market and might occur by reason of design. He knows that his wheat will be sold. He knows there will be a payment coming along and he knows that in the long run there is more stable marketing and a more stable income for him.
There is one point that we must remember. We cannot blame the wheat board for that which sometimes appears to be impossible for them to do. We must recognize that, while the wheat board is the only avenue through which the farmer can market his wheat, the wheat board must go out into a very competitive world, particularly at a time when there is no international wheat agreement in existence. The wheat board has to go out into what might be termed an open market among the nations of the world. Therefore the board goes out into a competitive market. It may not be able to do all that might be desired and we must not blame the board for minor failures which we might suppose it has made. If the board has not met all the wishes of the wheat grower I do not know that it is always and altogether the fault of the board. It could be by reason of circumstances that exist in the world and over which they have little control.

However, we do know that the world is in need of wheat. Wheat is a very stable food and perhaps the world would starve if it were not for the wheat supplies that come from the farms. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smith), the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), and a few minutes ago the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), and the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn), all being members of this group, have placed upon the record a good deal of valuable material as to the position which this group takes with respect to the wheat board, with respect to the farmer's position and with respect to the marketing of wheat generally. I believe the hon. member for Acadia mentioned the fact that the world needs wheat. The Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of November 9, 1956, points out that while the world carry-over of wheat is 1| billion bushels-at that time-the population of the world stands at 2| billion people; so 1J billion bushels represents only 36 pounds of wheat per person. In the United States 190 pounds of wheat per person are consumed annually. The annual world consumption of wheat is about 6 billion bushels. So a carry-over of 1J billion bushels is equivalent to only a three months' supply for wheat-eating nations.
The need for the reserve is further highlighted by a speech made by the North American representative of the food and agricultural organization, Mr. Hambridge. He pointed out that over 50 per cent of the population of the world are underfed and underclothed with millions dying from starvation. Then he made the significant statement that the situation would be bad enough if the people knew that it could not be avoided owing to a shortage of food in the world. But, he pointed out, they know that that is not the situation and they know that there is an abundance of food in the world. Hence they are no longer willing passively to submit to this intolerable situation.
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, the fact that sometimes it may be difficult to find markets but I am rather of the opinion that sometimes that difficulty exists because we are not always willing to take the various currencies of the world. We have two policies to propose. One is that we would be willing to go out into the world and offer credits to other nations who care to take our wheat. That has been done with some other countries. I think I am right in saying that that is the way in which the United States handled a good deal of their surplus wheat. There is no reason why we cannot do the same thing.

The wheat would be taken from the farmers, and the farmers would be paid for it, and we would be paid for it in the currencies of the nations that take our wheat. So in that respect it is not necessarily a wheat-marketing problem as much as it is a financial problem. This government here should embark upon a solution of that particular financial problem.
We advocate also a two-price system. We advocate that support prices should be maintained at 100 per cent of parity for farm products sold in the domestic market and that the surplus products should be sold abroad for the best price obtainable, preferably under some form of international agreement but in any event covered by a support price sufficient to meet average costs of production.
In view of the fact that over 94 per cent of all farm products, excluding wheat, are sold in Canada it would mean that farmers would receive 100 per cent of parity for 94 per cent of their products excluding wheat. In regard to wheat, approximately 80 per cent is sold abroad and 20 per cent is sold in the domestic market. Therefore 20 per cent at parity of, we will say, about $2.27 per bushel or thereabouts and 80 per cent at the ceiling of $1.95 per bushel under the international wheat agreement would give the farmers a support price of approximately $2 or a little over $2 a bushel.
We believe that careful consideration should be given to building up efficient family farms. Right now I want to put in a plug
Canadian Wheat Board Act for the small farmer. We believe that we should give consideration to building up efficient family farms. If it is conceded that family farms, in order to make the most efficient use of power machinery, will have to be in the neighbourhood of two sections of average land or one section of heavy land, and if the average annual production of wheat on such farms might be approximately 8,000 bushels of wheat, then we feel that by limiting the support price to 8,000 bushels per farmer we would help to strengthen the family farm. The large operators farming thousands of acres would receive the support price on the first 8,000 bushels and would receive the world market price on the balance.
I see that the clock has moved around to the point of ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I believe there are one or two others who wish to speak, but I am not through. I should like to spend the balance of the time that is allotted me to the furtherance of my speech, and I would ask that you call it ten o'clock. I move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Hansell the debate was adjourned.

1.	There are five poultry eviscerating plants in British Columbia operating as inspected establishments under the federal Meat and Canned Foods Act and receiving veterinary inspection by the health of animals division.
2.	The "Canada Approved" stamp, identifying the product of such inspected establishments, must be applied to all carcasses, cuts and packages of meats, including poultry, processed in those establishments, regardless of whether the products are to move in export, interprovincial or local trade.
3.	The provincial act provides for standards of plant sanitation, as a basis of accepting a plant under inspection, virtually equivalent to those established under the federal Meat and Canned Foods Act.
